chapter: Early recordings and arrival in New York
title: Benny Goodman band copying her 'Loch Lomond' with Martha Tilton
summary: Discussion of the Martha Tilton version and how Jimmy Mundy took the arrangement off her record while she was in New York; she is not resentful.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: There's also a record that you hear occasionally on the nostalgia stations of Martha Tilton.
I think probably from the 1938 Carnegie Hall Concert of Benny Goodman.
Yeah, well you know how that happened.
You personally, were on the west coast at that time?
No. The band was on the road. And when Benny Goodman left the city, there was no such person as Maxine Sullivan around.
So while they were out on the road -- I imagined they stopped in some little town and put a nickle in the juke box and they heard this recording

of 'Loch Lomond.' So Jimmy Mundy took the arrangement off the record. And when they came to New York and did the concert at Carnegie Hall, and Martha Tilton sang it, you know, they thought they were introducing somebody, and I was singing it on second speed. So that got to be a big joke too, you know.
Do you feel resentful about that?

No! I mean we knew what happened. It couldn't hurt. You know, the more recordings of 'Loch Lomond,' the more popular it was going to make me. And the controversy didn't hurt either. I left Leo Fitzpatrick years later, and I told him -- I said, 'You're the one who turned me off the air.' He said, 'Well it didn't hurt you a bit.' And it didn't.
